network.overall_strategy: This is a connected candidate synthesis network, not an experimentally validated end-to-end production process. The supplied evidence does not establish ten independent, complete prebiotic syntheses of free arginine. Accordingly, the ten pathways below are explicitly differentiated reaction sequences: eight variants of the cyanosulfidic scaffold and two ornithine-source pathways. They are not presented as ten experimentally demonstrated routes. The strongest scaffold follows Patel et al. (2015) to the arginine alpha-aminonitrile; conversion to free arginine remains an unquantified endpoint under the proposed environmental conditions. Copper-free initial photoreductions, substrate-specific sulfite substitutions, and alkaline endpoint processing are identified as hypotheses. The ornithine pathways distinguish discharge-derived material from isotope-supported heterogeneous synthesis of ornithine; neither assumes that the contested historical direct-arginine assignment is secure. Unsupported peptide assembly, terminal thioamide substitutions, and an invented glutamate-to-ornithine bridge are excluded. Unless explicitly identified as reported evidence, numerical conditions are proposed screening windows, not literature-validated operating recipes or predictions of successful conversion. Staged reagent delivery is necessary: ammonia-rich addition, cyanamide trapping, sulfide photochemistry, and hydrolysis must not be assumed compatible in one pot. Photochemical steps require measured spectral irradiance, dissolved-metal speciation, sulfur availability, and losses to abundant Fe2+; these quantities are presently unresolved. Neutral molecular formulas describe parent structures rather than dominant aqueous protonation states; sulfite and sulfate charges are explicit. S8 is a formal sulfur oxidation-product balance, not a claim that all photochemical sulfur becomes cyclooctasulfur. Discharge and heterogeneous source reactions are coarse-grained product-channel projections, not selective elementary reactions or complete mixture mass balances. No enantioenrichment is assumed. The environment_formed field gives the principal formation setting; reaction nodes specify alternative settings. No overall yield, productive residence time, or transport recovery is established.

reactions.name: Cu(I)-mediated acetylene hydrocyanation

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with a gas-retaining headspace
conditions.catalyst: Cu(I), with actual dissolved speciation measured
conditions.other: Proposed starting concentrations: 1-20 mM total cyanide, 1-20 mM dissolved acetylene, and 10-100 micromolar total Cu. Screen pH 6-8 and 1-24 h residence. Exclude O2 and sulfide during this entry step. Gas dissolution, HCN escape, copper precipitation, and acrylonitrile polymerization must be quantified.

reactions.mechanism: Copper-mediated net addition of HCN across the acetylene triple bond forms acrylonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: This is the documented entry to the arginine/proline branch in Patel et al. (2015). Cu(I) is assigned for its specific coupling role, not because a generic copper mineral guarantees catalysis. The supplied report does not provide an exact reproducible protocol for these numerical conditions. Cyanide accumulation remains conditional; Toner and Catling (2019) support storage and concentration mechanisms, not automatic delivery of the proposed dissolved concentrations.

reactions.name: Ammonia conjugate addition to acrylonitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm, gas-retaining pool or headspace
conditions.other: Proposed 1-10 mM acrylonitrile and 20-200 mM total ammonia/ammonium, pH 9-10.5, for 1-48 h. Establish conversion before dilution into the photochemical stage. Monitor multiple alkylation and oligomerization rather than assuming exclusive monoaddition.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia undergoes aza-Michael addition to the activated alkene, furnishing beta-aminopropionitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support this carbon-nitrogen bond-forming step. Concentrated ammonia is a local environmental requirement, not an assumed ocean composition. Excess ammonia useful here can interfere with later cyanamide allocation, requiring actual measurements of reagent carryover.

reactions.name: Early guanidination of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.other: Proposed 1-10 mM aminonitrile and 1-50 mM cyanamide, pH 8.5-10, sampled over 1 h to 7 days. Quantify starting-material retention, cyanamide hydrolysis, and dimerization. Do not assign all downstream guanidinated product to this step when residual cyanamide remains.

reactions.mechanism: The terminal amine attacks cyanamide carbon; proton transfer and tautomerization produce the substituted guanidine.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) explicitly describe direct guanidination at this stage as relatively inefficient. This pathway is retained as a chemically distinct observed possibility, not as an equally productive alternative to aldehyde-stage capture. Its fractional contribution requires intermediate-resolved measurements.

reactions.name: Cu-assisted sulfidic photoreduction of beta-aminopropionitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted H2S loss
conditions.other: Proposed 1-10 mM substrate, 1-30 mM total dissolved sulfide, 10-100 micromolar total Cu, and pH 7-9. Use a shallow optical path of at most 1 cm. A 254 nm laboratory comparator is supported by the research; proposed environmental testing uses measured 200-280 nm irradiation at 0.01-0.1 mW/cm2 for 1-24 h. Supply cyanamide promptly for rxn_010. Determine dissolved Cu and sulfide after contact with Fe2+-bearing material.

reactions.mechanism: Photochemical reducing equivalents convert the nitrile to an imine-level intermediate; hydrolysis releases ammonia and beta-aminopropionaldehyde. Sulfide supplies reducing equivalents.
reactions.reasoning: The transformation follows Patel et al. (2015). The stated concentrations, irradiance, and exposure times are prospective, not a reproduced branch-specific protocol. Ranjan et al. (2018) constrain attainable sulfide concentrations and UV transmission; Ranjan and Sasselov (2017) support surface UV availability but not equivalence between sunlight and a 254 nm lamp. Copper sulfide precipitation and FeS formation can remove the assumed active reagents.

reactions.name: Cu-assisted photoreduction of the early guanidinated nitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted H2S loss
conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM guanidinated nitrile, 1-30 mM dissolved sulfide, 10-100 micromolar total Cu, pH 7-9, and 1-24 h irradiation. Use a 254 nm comparator and separately measured 200-280 nm surface-like exposure. Resolve the cyclic hemiaminal from residual starting material and products formed by aldehyde-stage cyanamide capture.

reactions.mechanism: Nitrile photoreduction and hydrolysis generate a guanidinated aldehyde that can close intramolecularly to a six-membered hemiaminal.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support the early-guanidination branch within the connected chemistry, but mixed reaction products do not establish its isolated flux or efficiency. The cyclic node represents an aldehyde-equivalent structure; its tautomer and stereoisomer distribution is not assigned an unverified InChI. Sulfur and copper availability remain subject to the constraints discussed by Ranjan et al. (2018).

reactions.name: Copper-free sulfidic entry photoreduction

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted H2S loss
conditions.other: Proposed 1-10 mM aminonitrile, 5-30 mM sulfide, pH 7-9, and 1-48 h irradiation. Compare a 254 nm lamp with measured 200-280 nm exposure at 0.01-0.1 mW/cm2. Verify removal of copper carried from rxn_001; do not assume natural quantitative metal separation. Later photochemical steps in this pathway may still require Cu.

reactions.mechanism: Direct sulfide photochemistry is proposed to provide reducing equivalents for nitrile-to-aldehyde conversion without added copper.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for this substrate under these conditions. Patel et al. (2015) and the supplied research indicate that some related sulfidic reductions can occur without copper, but that does not establish this arginine-branch reaction's rate or selectivity. The alternative has chemical merit where copper precipitates, but only if sufficient unscavenged sulfide and usable photons remain; Ranjan et al. (2018) identify that supply constraint.

reactions.name: Copper-free photoreduction of the early guanidinated nitrile

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted H2S loss
conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM substrate, 5-30 mM sulfide, pH 7-9, and 1-48 h irradiation with the same measured spectral comparison used for rxn_006. Measure guanidino-group retention, substrate disappearance, and hemiaminal formation independently.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed direct sulfidic photoreduction of the nitrile is followed by hydrolysis and intramolecular hemiaminal formation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate-specific extension of related copper-free photochemistry discussed around Patel et al. (2015). Neither the inefficient early guanidination nor general availability of photochemical electrons demonstrates this edge. It is retained as a testable catalyst-dependence alternative, not as a demonstrated improvement.

reactions.name: Sulfite-driven entry photoreduction

conditions.other: Proposed 1-10 mM aminonitrile, 1-30 mM total sulfite/bisulfite, pH 8-9, and 1-48 h irradiation. Compare 254 nm irradiation with measured 200-280 nm surface-like exposure. Exclude O2 and measure carbonyl-bisulfite trapping, hydrated-electron scavenging, sulfate formation, and cyanamide compatibility.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfite photoionization is proposed to supply reducing equivalents; nitrile reduction and hydrolysis produce the aldehyde. Sulfate provides a balanced net oxidation endpoint for the sulfur donor.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative for beta-aminopropionitrile. Ranjan et al. (2018) support potentially more favorable sulfite availability and motivate alternative sulfur photochemistry, but do not validate this substrate conversion or its product distribution. Sulfate is a net balance, not a claim of exclusive sulfur speciation. Sulfide is still required downstream for thioamide formation.

reactions.name: Sulfite-driven photoreduction of the early guanidinated nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM guanidinated nitrile, 1-30 mM sulfite/bisulfite, pH 8-9, and 1-48 h measured UV exposure. Determine whether carbonyl trapping, guanidino photochemistry, or sulfur-radical addition competes with the intended conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed sulfite-derived reducing equivalents convert the nitrile to an aldehyde equivalent, followed by cyclic hemiaminal formation.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative. Ranjan et al. (2018) provide environmental motivation, not substrate-specific experimental support. Patel et al. (2015) support the surrounding scaffold but not this substitution. This pathway therefore carries both the early-guanidination bottleneck and an unvalidated photoreduction.

reactions.name: Aldehyde-stage cyanamide capture and guanidino hemiaminal formation

conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM freshly generated aldehyde and 1-30 mM cyanamide, pH 7-9. Introduce cyanamide during or immediately after aldehyde generation; sample from minutes to 24 h. Quantify aldehyde degradation, hemiaminal formation, and remaining cyanamide before further HCN addition.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanamide engages the aldehyde and the tethered amine in a coupled addition/cyclization sequence, furnishing a guanidinated cyclic hemiaminal that acts as an open-chain aldehyde reservoir.
reactions.reasoning: This is the better-supported guanidination timing in Patel et al. (2015), where photogenerated aldehyde capture was much more effective than direct guanidination of the aminonitrile. The paper's qualitative rapid trapping does not establish a numerical rate constant for the proposed pool composition. Maintaining cyanamide availability despite rxn_024 and rxn_025 is a necessary kinetic condition.

reactions.name: First cyanide homologation of the guanidinated aldehyde equivalent

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted HCN loss
conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM hemiaminal and 1-20 mM total cyanide, pH 7.5-9, for 0.5-24 h in a dark or shielded mixing compartment. Measure the reversible ring-opening/cyanohydrin equilibrium rather than assuming complete conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Reversible opening of the cyclic hemiaminal exposes the aldehyde; cyanide addition and proton transfer extend the carbon skeleton by one carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support HCN homologation of the guanidinated aldehyde-derived branch. Explicit ring opening avoids treating the isolated hemiaminal as though it were an unencumbered free aldehyde. Local cyanide concentration and retention are additional requirements, consistent with the motivation for storage mechanisms in Toner and Catling (2019).

reactions.name: Sulfide addition to form the alpha-hydroxythioamide

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted H2S loss
conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM cyanohydrin and 5-30 mM dissolved sulfide, pH 7-9, for 1-48 h. Begin without irradiation to distinguish sulfur incorporation from later photochemistry. Determine sulfide consumption by Fe2+ and copper before interpreting nominal reagent concentrations.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrosulfide attacks the nitrile carbon; proton transfers produce the alpha-hydroxythioamide.
reactions.reasoning: This sulfur-incorporating step belongs to the demonstrated homologation chemistry in Patel et al. (2015). Sulfite cannot be substituted merely because it can sometimes supply photochemical electrons: a reduced sulfur atom is incorporated here. Ranjan et al. (2018) therefore remain relevant even for pathways using sulfite at the entry reduction.

reactions.name: Photochemical deoxygenation of the alpha-hydroxythioamide

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted H2S loss
conditions.catalyst: Cu(I)/Cu(II) photoredox species, where maintained in an active form
conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM hydroxythioamide, 1-30 mM sulfide, 10-100 micromolar total Cu, pH 7-9, and 1-24 h irradiation. Compare a 254 nm laboratory benchmark with measured surface-like irradiation. Monitor thioamide cleavage, guanidino retention, sulfur turbidity, and optical attenuation.

reactions.mechanism: Photoreductive C-O cleavage replaces the alpha-hydroxyl group with hydrogen, retaining the thioamide needed for subsequent chain extension.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support this hydroxythioamide-to-thioamide homologation stage. The balanced S8 output represents the reductant oxidation requirement, not demonstrated sulfur-product selectivity. Neither a constant photon dose nor constant dissolved copper can be presumed as sulfur precipitates accumulate.

reactions.name: Thioamide photoreduction and hydrolysis to the homologated aldehyde

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted H2S loss
conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM thioamide, a maintained 1-30 mM sulfide pool, 10-100 micromolar total Cu, pH 7-9, and 1-24 h irradiation. Sample aldehyde formation before adding the next HCN pulse. Determine actual sulfur speciation and ammonia release.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped photoreduction/hydrolysis module converts the thioamide carbon into an aldehyde. H2S is included on both sides to represent reductant participation followed by sulfide release from the substrate; cancellation gives the formal net sulfur-extrusion balance.
reactions.reasoning: The further reduction to an aldehyde equivalent follows the homologation sequence described by Patel et al. (2015). This reaction node does not claim that the written net balance identifies every elementary intermediate or the measured sulfur distribution. Treating it as a module is more defensible than inventing isolated mechanistic intermediates not established in the supplied research.

reactions.name: Second cyanide homologation to the arginine carbon skeleton

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted HCN loss
conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM aldehyde and 1-20 mM total cyanide, pH 7.5-9, for 0.5-24 h after the photoreduction stage. Limit further irradiation during addition and quantify reversible cyanohydrin formation.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide addition to the homologated aldehyde establishes the five-carbon amino-acid backbone; the guanidino carbon accounts for the sixth carbon of arginine.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support the second HCN addition in the arginine-precursor branch. Explicit carbon accounting distinguishes backbone homologation from guanidino-group installation and avoids an unexplained jump in molecular size.

reactions.name: Strecker-type conversion of the final cyanohydrin to arginine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM cyanohydrin and 20-200 mM total ammonia/ammonium, pH 8.5-10, for 1-48 h. Use a dark mixing stage after photochemistry. Quantify aminonitrile, residual cyanohydrin, and cyclic or hydrolyzed products.

reactions.mechanism: Through reversible carbonyl/imine chemistry and cyanide capture, ammonia replaces the cyanohydrin hydroxyl functionality in the net reaction, yielding the alpha-aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) identify compound 46 as the arginine alpha-aminonitrile precursor. This is the experimentally strongest arginine-specific endpoint in the supplied de novo literature. It must not be equated with an isolated or quantitatively recovered free-arginine product.

reactions.name: Acidic hydration of arginine aminonitrile to argininamide
agents: Hydronium from an anoxic volcanic acid source

conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM aminonitrile, pH 1-2 maintained by volcanic acid input, and sampling over 1 h to 30 days. This is a separate shielded hydrolysis stage after photochemistry. Measure retro-Strecker loss, amide accumulation, guanidino retention, and total nitrogen balance. No productive residence time is established.

reactions.mechanism: Acid activation of the nitrile permits water addition and tautomerization to the corresponding primary amide.
reactions.reasoning: Conventional nitrile chemistry supports this mechanistic expectation, but the proposed environmental operating step is unvalidated. Patel et al. (2015) establish the aminonitrile precursor, not a substrate-specific hydration rate or argininamide yield under these conditions. Mild volcanic acidity is specified rather than silently assuming concentrated laboratory acid; whether it is sufficient before competing decomposition is a central bottleneck.

reactions.name: Acidic hydrolysis of argininamide to free arginine
agents: Hydronium from an anoxic volcanic acid source

conditions.other: Maintain pH 1-2 and sample 0.1-10 mM amide over 1-30 days, followed by cooling to 300-320 K. Ammonia is predominantly ammonium in situ. Quantify free arginine against an authentic standard and independently measure ornithine, urea, remaining amide, and other degradation products. Recovery during neutralization or concentration is unknown.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalyzed amide hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid functionality and releases ammonia/ammonium.
reactions.reasoning: Chemically conventional but unvalidated as this network's geochemical endpoint. The supplied Patel et al. (2015) evidence does not provide an end-to-end isolated free-arginine yield. Specifying a plausible acid pool does not establish favorable competition between amide hydrolysis, substrate destruction, and dilution. Both rxn_017 and rxn_018 require direct kinetic and isotope-dilution product measurements.

reactions.name: Alkaline hydrothermal hydration of arginine aminonitrile
agents: Hydroxide supplied by alkaline water-rock chemistry

conditions.catalyst: Hydroxide; no mineral-specific catalytic enhancement assumed
conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM aminonitrile and pH 10-11 referenced to a cooled 298 K aliquot. Screen 1-30 days in a UV-shielded alkaline pore or flow-through zone. Transport from surface photochemistry must be measured; no concentration preservation is assumed. Track racemization, nitrile loss, guanidino degradation, and amide formation.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-promoted nitrile hydration produces the amide, written in neutral-parent molecular bookkeeping.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative operating alternative based on general nitrile hydrolysis chemistry, not an experiment reported by Patel et al. (2015). It has a distinct environmental rationale where alkaline heated water is available but strong acidity is not. Its disadvantages are slow hydration at modest alkalinity and potentially accelerated destruction of the desired functionality. It is not evidence that a submarine vent can perform the UV-dependent upstream sequence.

reactions.name: Alkaline hydrothermal hydrolysis of argininamide
agents: Hydroxide supplied by alkaline water-rock chemistry

conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM amide, cooled-aliquot pH 10-11, and 1-30 days of sampling. Product is predominantly carboxylate in situ. Cool and remove product from prolonged heating where possible, while measuring recovery rather than assuming it. Reject this branch if guanidino loss or other decomposition outruns amide hydrolysis.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-promoted acyl substitution releases ammonia and generates the amino-acid carboxylate; the displayed formula is the neutral parent.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a selective prebiotic endpoint. No supplied study validates argininamide-to-arginine conversion under this alkaline hydrothermal window. Patel et al. (2015) support the upstream precursor only. Alkaline processing is therefore a testable alternative, not a resolution of the missing free-arginine demonstration.

reactions.name: Volcanic discharge production and aqueous recovery of an ornithine-containing fraction

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas-water system; transient discharge channels are much hotter
conditions.other: Anoxic methane/ammonia/water-vapor discharge with hot-water mist and a 300-330 K condensate collector. Proposed source-screening duration is 1-7 days; no particular gas ratio or ornithine concentration is established by the supplied summary. This node includes product collection and any necessary analytical hydrolysis. Downstream guanidination requires measured ornithine recovery and concentration, not direct use of an uncharacterized tar mixture.

reactions.mechanism: Coarse-grained discharge-driven radical chemistry, carbon-chain growth, nitrogen incorporation, condensation, and aqueous processing generate a broad mixture containing an ornithine channel. The displayed balance is not an elementary methane-to-ornithine reaction.
reactions.reasoning: Johnson et al. (2008) support the expanded amino-acid inventory of the volcanic-discharge apparatus; the supplied review attributes ornithine occurrence to that work and subsequent analyses. This supports a possible ornithine source, not a selective route, a measured environmental yield, or a demonstrated connection to cyanamide guanidination. Unresolved intermediates are not invented to imply mechanistic completeness.

reactions.name: Heterogeneous CO/H2/NH3 production and recovery of an ornithine-containing fraction

conditions.temperature: 473-600 K proposed gas-solid stage, followed by 300-330 K collection
conditions.pressure: 10-50 bar proposed terrestrial adaptation; the supplied research summary does not specify the historical experimental pressure
conditions.catalyst: Nickel-bearing surface with accessible reduced metal
conditions.other: Anoxic CO/H2/NH3 flow over a characterized metal surface, with immediate transfer to a cooler collector and aqueous workup. Screen 1-24 h hot-zone exposure without assuming an established optimum. The historical experiments covered 473-973 K; ornithine formation specifically within the proposed narrower range and elevated pressure is unvalidated. Sulfur poisoning, competing hydrocarbons, and amino-acid survival must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved heterogeneous carbon reduction/coupling and nitrogen-incorporation chemistry generates a complex product mixture. The written reaction is a formal ornithine-producing channel, not a selective Fischer-Tropsch elementary step.
reactions.reasoning: Yoshino et al. (1971) reported broad amino-acid synthesis, and Hayatsu et al. (1971) included ornithine among isotope/mass-spectrometry-confirmed products. Arginine was not in that confirmed list, so this node deliberately supplies ornithine rather than asserting direct arginine synthesis. The high-pressure terrestrial mapping and lower-temperature subset are speculative adaptations, and the historical very low amino-acid yields prevent assuming useful downstream concentrations.

reactions.name: Free-ornithine delta-amine guanidination by cyanamide

conditions.other: Proposed 0.1-10 mM analytically verified ornithine and 1-50 mM cyanamide, pH 9-10.5, sampled over 6 h to 7 days. Compare limited cyanamide pulses with excess reagent. Quantify alpha- versus delta-guanidination, overguanidination, cyanamide loss, lactam formation, and effects of Fe2+, salts, and residual ammonia from source mixtures. Concentration and source-to-pool transfer recovery are unknown.

reactions.mechanism: The ornithine delta-amine attacks cyanamide carbon, followed by proton transfer and tautomerization to the arginine guanidino group.
reactions.reasoning: Longo et al. (2020) strongly support chemical ornithine-to-arginine conversion in peptide contexts and discuss simple guanidinating reagents, but their complete peptide conversion is not evidence for this free-ornithine/cyanamide environmental protocol. Steinman et al. (1964) establish cyanamide's broader prebiotic reactivity, not a quantitative arginine yield. Free ornithine has two competing amino groups, so selective production of arginine is a central unresolved requirement rather than an assumed outcome.

reactions.name: Competing cyanamide hydrolysis

conditions.other: Monitor alongside productive reactions over their actual pH and residence-time histories, with proposed initial cyanamide concentrations of 1-50 mM. Sample from hours to weeks; do not assign one universal hydrolysis rate across acidic, neutral, and alkaline stages.

reactions.mechanism: Water addition to cyanamide and proton transfers form urea.
reactions.reasoning: This chemically established competing sink is included because cyanamide is not an inexhaustible reagent. Steinman et al. (1964) support its finite aqueous lifetime and competing reactivity in chemical-evolution chemistry, but the supplied literature does not determine the sink rate in the proposed arginine mixtures. Rate competition must be measured rather than inferred from thermodynamic favorability.

reactions.name: Competing cyanamide dimerization

conditions.other: Track during cyanamide concentration and guanidination at pH 8-10.5, particularly with 10-50 mM or more concentrated cyanamide. Sample over 1 h to 7 days and through partial evaporation. The cyanamide coefficient is inferred rather than represented by repeating its molecule ID.

reactions.mechanism: One cyanamide molecule adds to another, giving cyanoguanidine, commonly called dicyandiamide.
reactions.reasoning: A plausible and chemically established cyanamide sink, included to prevent unlimited allocation of the same reagent to productive branches. The supplied report identifies dicyandiamide formation as a necessary measurement, but provides no applicable rate constants. Steinman et al. (1964) support cyanamide's competing condensation chemistry; they do not validate this network's predicted partitioning.

reactions.name: Competing ornithine delta-lactam formation

conditions.other: Partially dry ornithine-containing films formed from initially pH 7-9 solutions. Proposed comparison: 1-3 wet-dry cycles with 8-24 h dry phases. These times are not asserted to reproduce the cited protocol. Measure lactamization during any source-concentration step rather than treating evaporation as loss-free.

reactions.mechanism: Intramolecular attack of the delta-amine on the carboxyl group eliminates water and forms a six-membered lactam.
reactions.reasoning: Frenkel-Pinter et al. (2019) demonstrate the importance of ornithine lactamization during prebiotic dry-down chemistry. This connected sink is why the network does not manufacture an unsupported productive ornithine-peptide route merely to increase the pathway count. A useful ornithine-first pathway must outcompete or avoid this loss during concentration.

reactions.name: Competing alpha-amine guanidination of free ornithine

conditions.other: Use the same 0.1-10 mM ornithine, 1-50 mM cyanamide, pH 9-10.5, and 6 h to 7 day time course as rxn_023. Separate regioisomers chromatographically and confirm connectivity; exact mass alone cannot distinguish this product from arginine.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-amine, rather than the delta-amine, attacks cyanamide to produce the constitutional guanidination isomer.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative competing channel included on functional-group chemistry grounds; no supplied study quantifies it for free ornithine plus cyanamide. Longo et al. (2020) demonstrate useful selectivity in particular peptide substrates, but those observations cannot be transferred quantitatively to an unprotected free diamino acid. Explicitly representing this isomer prevents equating a C6H14N4O2 analytical signal with confirmed arginine.

pathways.name: Aldehyde-stage guanidination with Cu/sulfide photochemistry and acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Strongest supplied de novo scaffold: construct beta-aminopropionaldehyde, trap it with cyanamide, homologate through thioamides, and form arginine aminonitrile. Acidic hydration and amide hydrolysis are chemically conventional but unvalidated under the proposed pool conditions. This is not a demonstrated complete free-arginine synthesis.

pathways.name: Early guanidination with Cu/sulfide photochemistry and acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Guanidination precedes the first nitrile reduction. This differs from P1 in reaction order and intermediate identity, but Patel et al. report inefficient early guanidination. Its productive contribution must be distinguished from subsequent aldehyde capture by residual cyanamide. The acidic free-arginine endpoint remains unvalidated.

pathways.name: Copper-free entry reduction followed by aldehyde-stage guanidination
pathways.description: Tests whether direct sulfidic photochemistry can replace Cu assistance for the initial aminonitrile reduction. Only that entry reduction is copper-free; the acetylene coupling and subsequent photochemical stages still use Cu. Substrate-specific conversion and environmental metal separation are unresolved, in addition to the terminal hydrolysis gap.

pathways.name: Early guanidination followed by copper-free entry reduction
pathways.description: Combines the experimentally inefficient early guanidination branch with a speculative copper-free reduction of its product. The remaining homologation sequence is shared with the supported scaffold. Neither the proposed reduction nor quantitative free-arginine recovery has been demonstrated.

pathways.name: Sulfite entry reduction followed by aldehyde-stage guanidination
pathways.description: Uses a speculative sulfite-driven reduction motivated by environmental sulfite availability. Sulfide remains necessary for thioamide formation and later sulfidic photochemistry. Carbonyl-bisulfite trapping and compatibility with cyanamide are additional bottlenecks; favorable sulfur supply alone does not validate the route.

pathways.name: Early guanidination followed by sulfite entry reduction
pathways.description: Tests sulfite photoreduction of the guanidinated nitrile rather than the unmodified aminonitrile. It is a distinct substrate/reductant hypothesis, not an experimentally established route. It combines inefficient early guanidination, unvalidated substrate-specific photochemistry, and the unresolved acidic free-arginine endpoint.

pathways.name: Aldehyde-stage guanidination followed by alkaline hydrothermal endpoint processing
pathways.description: Shares the strongest surface precursor scaffold with P1 but replaces acidic terminal hydrolysis with two alkaline hydrothermal transformations. These are different reaction conditions and catalytic channels, not a new carbon-skeleton synthesis. Transport losses and competition between hydrolysis and guanidino degradation must be measured before claiming completion.

pathways.name: Early guanidination followed by alkaline hydrothermal endpoint processing
pathways.description: Combines early guanidination with the alkaline endpoint alternative. It is distinguished from P2 by the hydrolysis regime and from P7 by guanidination timing. Both the inefficient entry branch and the selective alkaline production of free arginine require validation.

pathways.name: Volcanic-discharge ornithine followed by free-monomer guanidination
pathways.description: Uses a literature-supported abiotic ornithine source class, followed by the chemically plausible cyanamide guanidination cut. The source node is a mixture-generating module, not selective ornithine synthesis. Ornithine recovery, concentration without lactamization, and delta- versus alpha-guanidination are unresolved; Longo et al.'s peptide results do not close these gaps.

pathways.name: Heterogeneously synthesized ornithine followed by free-monomer guanidination
pathways.description: Uses isotope-supported historical ornithine formation from CO/H2/NH3 rather than the contested direct-arginine assignment. The proposed terrestrial pressure and temperature subset are unvalidated adaptations. Very low source selectivity, hot-zone survival, collection efficiency, and selective cyanamide guanidination prevent treating this as an established complete synthesis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest pathway on the supplied evidence. Patel et al. (2015) support the scaffold through the arginine alpha-aminonitrile, including effective aldehyde-stage cyanamide trapping. Acidic nitrile hydration and amide hydrolysis are chemically credible, but rxn_017 and rxn_018 lack a substrate-specific operating protocol and quantified free-arginine recovery. Their uncertainty is not a conservation violation or proof of chemical impossibility. Surface labels and acknowledgment of staging do not establish compatible reagent concentrations, irradiation, acidity, or residence times.
suggestions: Demonstrate both hydrolysis stages using the actual aminonitrile-containing reaction mixture, quantifying argininamide, free arginine, and competing products.
Specify staged pH, temperature, reagent concentrations, UV spectrum and dose, copper speciation, and intermediate recovery.
Attach reaction-level references and distinguish measured conditions from proposed environmental conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Early guanidination is chemically plausible, but Patel et al. describe it as relatively inefficient. Product formation after irradiation of a mixed guanidination reaction must not automatically be attributed to rxn_005: residual cyanamide can instead trap aldehyde produced from unguanidinated starting material. The isolated early-guanylated branch therefore needs clearer substrate-specific evidence and material accounting. The downstream scaffold is coherent, while free-arginine recovery remains unquantified.
suggestions: Measure rxn_003 conversion and determine how much downstream product originates from the early-guanylated versus aldehyde-trapping branch.
Validate rxn_005 with structurally authenticated mol_013 and quantify competing photochemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Copper-free sulfide photochemistry is plausible in principle, but the supplied literature does not establish adequate rate or selectivity for beta-aminopropionitrile reduction in rxn_006 under the proposed setting. The network correctly labels this substitution as hypothetical. Subsequent aldehyde trapping and homologation follow the stronger scaffold, but cannot compensate for an unvalidated entry reduction. This is not a wholly copper-free pathway because rxn_001 still requires Cu(I). Acidic endpoint recovery is also unresolved.
suggestions: Compare copper-assisted and copper-free rxn_006 conditions at matched spectral irradiance, sulfur concentration, and pH.
Measure aldehyde capture versus decomposition or cyclization, including effects of residual copper from rxn_001 and dissolved iron.
Demonstrate free-arginine production after the proposed acidic processing.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway combines inefficient early guanidination with an unvalidated copper-free reduction of the guanidinated nitrile. General evidence for sulfide photoreduction does not establish the substrate-specific behavior of mol_013, including its protonation, competing reactions, and productive hemiaminal formation. The later transformations remain chemically coherent, but the pathway lacks evidence that sufficient material reaches them. Free arginine is still an expected rather than demonstrated endpoint under the stated conditions.
suggestions: Test rxn_007 using authenticated mol_013 and appropriate dark, sulfur-free, and copper-assisted controls.
Distinguish genuine copper-free activity from residual copper carried over from rxn_001.
Quantify the early-guanidination material balance and subsequent acidic arginine recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ranjan et al. (2018) support the potential environmental availability of sulfite, but do not establish rxn_008 on this substrate. Its balanced redox equation is necessary but insufficient evidence for useful photochemical conversion. Sulfite/bisulfite interactions with the generated aldehyde may also affect cyanamide trapping. This substitution does not eliminate the reduced-sulfur requirements of the later thioamide chemistry. The final acidic hydrolysis sequence remains unquantified.
suggestions: Measure the action spectrum, aldehyde yield, and competing products of rxn_008 under specified sulfite speciation and pH.
Test whether sulfite/bisulfite carbonyl adducts interfere with rxn_010.
Specify reduced-sulfur delivery for downstream reactions and validate free-arginine recovery after hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The conserved stoichiometry of rxn_009 does not validate sulfite-driven reduction of the early-guanylated nitrile. This substrate-specific substitution is unsupported by the supplied experimental findings and follows an already inefficient guanidination step. The environmental motivation for sulfite is reasonable, but successful reduction, hemiaminal formation, and compatibility with subsequent sulfide chemistry remain hypotheses. The pathway correctly avoids claiming that sulfite replaces sulfur incorporation throughout the network.
suggestions: Establish rxn_009 conversion and selectivity with authenticated mol_013 rather than extrapolating from unrelated sulfite photoreductions.
Quantify early guanidination and test transfer from sulfite-containing mixtures into the downstream sulfide chemistry.
Demonstrate the acidic endpoint with an arginine-specific product balance.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The pathway retains the strongest precursor-forming scaffold, but alkaline hydrothermal processing introduces an unvalidated endpoint. Base-promoted nitrile and amide hydrolysis are chemically possible; however, no temperature-pH-residence-time window demonstrates selective arginine accumulation rather than competing substrate or product degradation. The concern is not the use of another environment, but the absence of specified phase conditions, transport recovery, and substrate-specific hydrolysis selectivity.
suggestions: Map aminonitrile hydration, argininamide hydrolysis, and arginine stability across defined temperature, pH, and residence-time conditions.
Quantify possible guanidino-group degradation and other products rather than measuring nitrile disappearance alone.
Specify heating, pressure, transfer, and cooling conditions with measured material recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway combines the material-throughput uncertainty of early guanidination with the unvalidated alkaline hydrothermal endpoint. Neither issue violates conservation, and the formal sequence reaches the correct target structure. Nevertheless, evidence for productive passage through rxn_003/rxn_005 and selective completion of rxn_019/rxn_020 is insufficient to establish free-arginine production. Environmental consistency cannot be verified from the broad setting labels alone.
suggestions: Validate the early-guanylated branch separately from residual-cyanamide aldehyde trapping.
Measure alkaline endpoint conversion and arginine survival before integrating it with upstream photochemistry.
Provide a transfer and residence-time model that includes dilution, chemical losses, and cooling.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The supplied volcanic-discharge literature supports an abiotic ornithine source, but not a selective source reaction or quantified delivery to guanidination. Cyanamide-mediated amine guanidination is plausible, yet Longo et al. (2020) do not establish selective free-ornithine-to-arginine conversion under these conditions. Free ornithine has competing alpha and delta amines. Including cyanamide losses, lactamization, and N-alpha-guanylornithine is appropriate, but does not establish their rates or the target selectivity.
suggestions: Quantify free ornithine in the collected discharge fraction and identify any hydrolysis, extraction, or concentration required before guanidination.
Measure delta- versus alpha-guanidination, cyanamide consumption, and lactam formation under a defined aqueous or wet-dry protocol.
Use authentic standards and structural analysis capable of distinguishing arginine from mol_030; molecular formula or nominal mass alone is insufficient.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hayatsu, Studier and Anders (1971) provide isotope-supported evidence for heterogeneous ornithine synthesis, so this pathway appropriately avoids relying on the contested direct-arginine assignment. However, that evidence does not establish selective ornithine production in an unspecified hydrothermal aqueous setting. The reported hot heterogeneous chemistry requires explicit catalyst, phase, pressure, collection, and workup conditions. Subsequent free-monomer guanidination retains the selectivity and reagent-competition uncertainties of P9.
suggestions: Specify how the reaction environment reproduces a supported mineral/gas synthesis regime rather than assuming that a Hydrothermal label establishes compatibility.
Determine whether free ornithine or hydrolysable precursors are recovered, and quantify cooling, collection, extraction, and concentration losses.
Test the recovered mixture directly in cyanamide guanidination, including alpha-guanidination and cyanamide-loss controls.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally sound: all 30 molecule nodes participate, molecule IDs are used consistently, and the productive modules and competing branches form a connected graph. The deterministic check establishes that all 27 reactions conserve atoms and charge with suitable coefficients; there are no UNBALANCED reactions. Factors of eight associated with formal S8 bookkeeping are not intrinsically implausible. H2S appearing on both sides of rxn_014 is cancelable bookkeeping, not a conservation violation, although actual sulfur products and reductant turnover require measurement. Literature alignment is strongest through the Patel et al. (2015) arginine alpha-aminonitrile scaffold. The network appropriately distinguishes that demonstrated precursor from an unquantified free-arginine endpoint, labels substrate-specific photochemical substitutions as hypotheses, and separates isotope-supported ornithine synthesis from the contested historical arginine assignment. However, transparency about uncertainty does not experimentally resolve it. The principal limitations are selective endpoint hydrolysis, substrate-specific support for alternative photoreductions, free-ornithine guanidination selectivity, and quantitative environmental integration. Only broad environment labels are supplied, without sufficient pH, temperature, pressure, concentration, irradiation, catalyst-speciation, or residence-time specifications to verify compatibility. The competing branches are sensible: rxn_024 represents cyanamide hydrolysis; rxn_025 requires two cyanamide molecules for dimerization; rxn_026 is supported particularly under concentrating or dry-down conditions rather than being established for arbitrary dilute surface water; and rxn_027 correctly represents a constitutional isomer distinct from arginine. Their inclusion improves chemical accounting, but their rates remain unknown. Reaction-level citations, explicit structures, and an end-to-end product and transport balance are needed. Scores reflect network-level bottlenecks, not pathway counts, shared intermediates, or the number or order of environments. This is a credible candidate network with notable unresolved chemistry and environmental requirements, but it does not meet the 0.9 network approval threshold.
